prompts.prompt:
Use case: scientific-educational. Asset type: an editorial raster illustration for an adult statistics course, one of a consistent five-image series. Style: a carefully art-directed human-designed university textbook illustration, restrained ink drawing and very subtle screen-print texture, crisp intentional geometry, a warm ivory paper background (#f8f5ee), dark graphite (#263849), muted ink blue (#285777), and a small ochre accent (#b4874b). Atmosphere: calm, thoughtful, trustworthy, uncluttered. Landscape 3:2 composition with generous negative space, a single central teaching diagram, balanced margins. Fine hand-ink character should be subtle; labels must be clean typeset sans-serif, not fake handwriting. No image headline, paragraph, footnote, decorative objects, stock icons, visual metaphors, gradients, 3D, glossy surfaces, glow, cartoon characters, gratuitous arrows, ornamental border, logo, or watermark. Use large sparse labels that remain legible when the image is displayed at 360 pixels wide. All diagram elements are schematic, not a claimed plot of observed data. No invented numerical data. Limit to at most four short labels. The scientific geometry and meaning are more important than decorative texture.
Primary request: Lesson 1, explain a two-sided p-value as tail area under an assumed null distribution. Draw ONE symmetric smooth bell curve over a fine horizontal baseline. Put TWO equidistant thin vertical dashed threshold marks, one on each side of the center. The right mark denotes the observed statistic. Shade ONLY the outer area under the curve to the left of the left mark and to the right of the right mark with muted ochre fine hatching. The central area must remain unshaded paper. Both tails must be equal in area. No y-axis, numerical ticks, alpha cutoff, second curve, or central point. Exact labels, and only these: "Under the null" above the peak; "Observed" below the right threshold; "Both tails" below the center, with two very fine leader lines to the two shaded regions. This diagram must make it clear that both equally extreme tails contribute to the p-value.

Primary request: Lesson 2, show that power is the probability of detection under a specified alternative. Draw ONE smooth bell-shaped alternative distribution, with its peak somewhat right of a single thin vertical dashed decision boundary. There is only one curve and one horizontal baseline, no y-axis, numbers, tick marks, or null curve. The boundary cuts the left shoulder of the curve, leaving a smaller left region and a larger right region. Show both regions as actual areas UNDER the curve, not separate rectangles. The smaller area to the left of the boundary is sparse muted graphite hatching, the larger area to the right is a very light ink-blue fill with subtle fine hatching. Exact labels and only these: "Specified effect" above the curve, "Missed" under the left region, "Detected" under the right region, and "Decision boundary" below the dashed line. This is explicitly a one-sided schematic with detection to the right; do not add alpha/beta formulas or an effect estimate.

Primary request: Lesson 3, teach a confidence interval for a mean relative to a fixed benchmark. Draw ONE straight, sparse horizontal reference line. Put a thin vertical dashed ochre benchmark line to the left of the entire interval. Further right, draw a blue horizontal confidence-interval segment with two short vertical endpoint caps, and one dark blue estimate dot between the caps. Primary request: Lesson 4, explain that two independent groups contain different observational units. Draw TWO horizontal rows of five small simple outlined record cards, with ample spacing. Label the upper row "Group A" and the lower row "Group B". Each card has a single small circular record mark, with no text or numbers inside. Use five muted-blue record marks in the first row and five muted-ochre record marks in the second row. Keep cards identical in scale but the row's individual card positions should be slightly staggered so there is NO visual pairing or matching column. The two rows are clearly separated by generous empty space. No lines or arrows linking the rows, no record repeated between groups, no means, error bars, curves, counts printed, people, or causal arrows. Only the two specified labels. This is a spare schematic of separate samples, not actual ANES data. The focus is separate records belonging to distinct groups.

Primary request: Lesson 5, show that pairing preserves the same observational unit between earlier and later measurements. Draw FIVE thin, gently irregular ink-blue lines connecting exactly five small blue dots in a left column to exactly five matching dots in a right column, one dot at each endpoint and no dots anywhere else. Each line represents one unit; exactly one unique line per pair. Positions vary vertically to suggest different within-unit changes. Prefer nearly parallel modest upward or downward slopes with no confusing line crossings. Label the left column "Before" and the right column "After". Put the single label "Same unit" above one central line with a tiny unobtrusive leader. No arrows, numeric values, axes, curve, histogram, extra records, people, or second panel. Do not imply all changes are identical or add causal treatment imagery. This is five schematic pairs, not a plot of the eleven Grunfeld firms. The continuity of each unit must be immediately visible.
